newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon municipal poll rerun in capital on Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Gabon municipal poll rerun in capital on Sunday.

text.p: Gabon on Sunday will hold a municipal election in the capital Libreville after a chaotic poll in October was scrapped, but the opposition has expressed concern about the distribution of voting cards.

But the head of the electoral commission said on Saturday that preparations were complete for the vote in which the strongest parties are expected to be President Omar Bongo's and the opposition Woodcutters' Party of Father Paul M'Ba Abessole.
"We are ready. We have sent all out all the voting material. The distribution of voting cards took place two days ago and voter lists are posted in all centres," Gilbert Ngoulakia told Reuters.
A rerun will also take place in Fougamou, where a fight prevented voting on October 20. The election commission had scrapped results in Libreville, blaming organisational problems.
Oil-producer Gabon holds its much delayed parliamentary election on December 1. The election commission has repeatedly put back the date, citing lack of adequate preparations.
Bongo and his opposition rivals struck a peace deal in Paris in 1994 to defuse political tension that bloodied the start of the democratic experiment in the nation of 1.2 million people.
The accords, approved in 1995 by referendum, were designed to increase electoral transparency. Parliament's mandate ran out in May. A second parliamentary round is planned for December 15.

A statement from an opposition alliance including the Woodcutters' Party in the government daily L'Union expressed "serious concern" about the organisation of Sunday's poll. It cited a lack of centres for distributing voting cards.
Bongo's Gabonese Democratic Party and the Woodcutters won most of the seats decided in the October 20 poll.
Bongo became president in 1968 on the death of Gabon's independence president, Leon Mba, and set up a one-party state.
He began moves towards a multi-party system in 1990 after a rash of strikes and demonstrations by students and workers.
He won a five-year term in a disputed 1993 poll, defeating Abessole, a priest. Five people died in opposition protests.

Further clashes followed in 1994, in part to back demands for pay rises after the devaluation that year of the CFA franc used in much of French-speaking Africa. The official death toll was nine, the opposition put the toll at 38.
